schools.summary: Gregory the Great: it is the way of the wicked to charge the good with their own faults; holy men bear it with forbearance, and Job, seeing Eliphaz turn from comfort to upbraiding as a feigned comforter, maintains by his patience a type of the Church that endures such slanders and confutes them by reasoning.

Henry: both sides took the disputant's way of undervaluing one another; the saw of contention grows hotter the longer it is drawn, censures are retorted endlessly, but cui bono? — angry answers never convince the judgment.
Gill marks the plain occasion: as soon as Eliphaz had done speaking, Job stood up and made his reply.

Clarke lays out the argument: Job answers Eliphaz and through him all the friends who added to his misfortunes, shows how differently he would use them, details his sufferings, and consoles himself with the innocence of which he takes God to witness.

Ellicott sketches the speech: finding the argument useless Job ceases it, complains of his friends' conduct, enlarges again on his condition, appeals touchingly to heaven, and ends declaring his case desperate.

themes: the appeal from men to God

schools.summary: Gill: Job had heard such maxims reported many times, nothing new but crambe millies cocta, given the hearing and scarcely that, being inapplicable to him.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh 'rabboth' (much, amply sufficient) and read the friends as consolatores onerosi, troublesome comforters who cause amal instead of easing it; Ellicott: their words are trite rather than true — 'vacant chaff well meant for grain.'

Clarke: they see him afflicted and should console him, yet prove miserable comforters all; Wesley: these things are but vulgar and trivial, as are all creatures to a soul under deep conviction of sin.

Henry names the two faults — needless repetition (provoking from an adversary though necessary from a teacher) and unskilful application that mistook his case; and true of all creatures, miserable comforters are they all, only the blessed Spirit comforting effectually.

themes: I have heard many such things

schools.summary: Gill: 'words of wind' is Eliphaz's own reproach (ch. 15:2) retorted — swelling bubbles that should have a speedy end; better silent than speaking to no purpose.
Clarke renders 'words of air' and reads 'what emboldeneth thee' as a thrust at Eliphaz's ignorance of the business; Wesley hears impatience and marks that Job flings back the charge of ch. 15:2-3.
Ellicott: the sense is 'shall not vain words have an end?' — Eliphaz had contributed nothing new but merely reiterated what was said before, so his boldness rests on no fresh matter.

themes: shall vain words have an end

schools.summary: Gill reads 'I also could speak as ye do' as scornful concession, or as a question conscience would never let him answer with such big words and high tone.

Henry calls it a cutting reproof: Job bids the friends change places with him, since the wheel soon turns; it is easy to trample the fallen, and he shows what he could do — heap up words and shake the head — to make them feel their own hardness.
Clarke renders the future 'I also will speak,' and unfolds the menacing head-shake — dark insinuation that more lay behind — asking 'but would this be right?'

Ellicott leaves it doubtful whether v.4 stands in contrast to v.5 (heaping words against) or in parallel (condoling and sympathising), and notes the head-shaking here differs from the contempt of Ps. 22:7 and Isa. 37:22.

debates.question: Is Job's 'shake mine head at you' a gesture of contempt or of sympathy?

sides.position: contempt — heaping up words against them, as they against him
possibly sympathy — making himself their companion, in parallel with v.5

themes: I also could speak as ye do

schools.summary: Gill: Job would discharge the comforter's office he had once shown others (owned by Eliphaz, ch. 4:3-4), strengthening them with good words as God, an angel, or a fellow-saint strengthens the distressed.

Henry draws the duty owed the afflicted — strengthen their faith and patience, assuage their grief; good words cost nothing yet make broken bones rejoice, and those have the tongue of the learned who speak a word in season to the weary.
Clarke records Mr. Good's reversed rendering ('with my own mouth will I overpower you, till the quivering of my lips shall fail'), countenanced by the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic.

outliers.note: Notes Mr. Good's opposite rendering of the verse — 'with my own mouth will I overpower you, till the quivering of my lips shall fail' — turning Job's promised comfort into a threat to overwhelm them.

themes: I would strengthen you with my mouth

schools.summary: Gill takes both clauses inwardly: neither speaking to God in prayer nor to himself in soliloquy assuages his grief; he cannot comfort himself as he once comforted others.
Clarke: reprehensions of the friends' conduct will not mitigate his sufferings — replying gives no relief.
Ellicott renders simply, 'I cannot but reply, though to reply gives me no relief.'

Henry: Job is at a stand whether to smother his complaint or vent it, helped by neither — if he complains, censured as passionate; if silent, as sullen; every way stopped, and even good men have much ado not to think hard of God.

themes: though I speak my grief is not assuaged

schools.summary: Gill: God's afflicting hand had made Job weary of the world and of life, his troubles heavier than the sand of the sea and his strength unequal to them.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the alternating address (now of God in the third person, now to him directly): 'thou hast made desolate all my company' by destroying his children and servants and alienating his friends.

Clarke prefers Job's afflictions and the ruin of his family (noting the Vulgate and Mr. Good's 'struck apart all my witnesses'); Wesley: God has made him weary of complaining and of life, turning his society into desolation.

Henry: weary of speaking, forbearing, friends, life itself; his household killed and dispersed, even his worshipping company scattered, so he keeps his sabbaths in solitude — and God's hand is to be owned in it.
Gill: the wrinkles came not by age but by affliction, sinking his flesh and aging him before his time — of the body only, for his soul was without spot or wrinkle through grace.

Keil and Delitzsch fix the rare verb (binding, grasping, thence wrinkling), pointing to emaciation and elephantiasis; Ellicott: the wrinkles were a witness against him (cf. ch. 10:17), and in his friends' eyes seemed unquestionable proof of guilt.
Clarke: if the disease were elephantiasis, whose wrinkled skin names the leprosy, the words apply exactly; he gathers Houbigant's and Good's renderings while owning the verse's obscurity.

themes: thou hast filled me with wrinkles
the body as witness against him

schools.summary: Gill takes the tearing enemy to be God himself as Job's mistaken grief conceived him, insisting God hates none of his creatures and that this is only Job's darkened apprehension.

Keil and Delitzsch refer the gnashing to the envious men who rejoiced at Job's fall, to whom his uprightness had been a burden; Ellicott finds the language almost exceeding Job's earlier boldness, calling God his adversary, and thinks it must be understood of God.

Clarke supposes God permitted Satan to appear in horrible form, the following verses describing the tempter and his demons — else the figures are strained past bearing if referred to the friends; Wesley reads the sharpened eyes as the fierce look of one enraged.

Henry canvasses all three — Eliphaz whose words tore Job's name, Satan his hater terrifying him by apparitions, or God, of whom the words are rash, for he hates none of his creatures and it was Job's melancholy that so represented the terrors of the Almighty.

debates.question: Who is the enemy who tears Job in his wrath and gnashes with his teeth?

sides.position: God himself, so conceived by Job's darkened grief
Satan, permitted to appear in visible terror with his demons
the envious men who rejoice at his fall

outliers.note: Refuses to fix the enemy, canvassing all three — Eliphaz, Satan, or God as Job's melancholy conceived him — and letting each stand as possible.

themes: he teareth me in his wrath

schools.summary: Gill reads the gaping mouths and smiting cheeks as the friends' calumnies and contempt, and hears in them Ps. 22:13, making Job a type of Christ mocked and smitten and crucified.
Keil and Delitzsch insist Job means not the friends but the envious men about him, who make an opening with their mouth, smite his cheeks in contempt, and conspire together against him.
Wesley: his friends opened their mouths wide against him; in all this Job was a type of Christ, these very words used of the Passion (Ps. 22:13; Mic. 5:1).
Henry: all about him came with open mouth to swallow him, smote him on the cheek, and gathered in confederacy, even the abjects (Ps. 35:15); a type of Christ, whose face was smitten (Matt. 26:67).

debates.question: Are the mockers who gape and smite the cheek the three friends, or the envious crowd about Job?

sides.position: the three friends, loading him with scorn
the envious men around him, not the friends

schools.summary: Gill notes the singular 'the ungodly' (the evil one) and canvasses Satan, the friends, or the Sabeans and Chaldeans; the word may mean 'delivered bound,' true of Christ bound and handed to the high priest and governor.

Ellicott: 'the ungodly and the wicked' are the very terms Job retorts on his friends, who have earned them; Keil and Delitzsch carry the picture into the assault that follows, God having handed Job over.
Wesley: as Job was delivered into wicked hands, so Christ was delivered into wicked hands by the determinate counsel of God (Acts 2:23).

debates.question: To whom has God delivered Job — who are 'the ungodly' and 'the wicked'?

sides.position: the friends, whose own favourite terms Job flings back at them
Satan, or the plundering Sabeans and Chaldeans

themes: Job a type of Christ betrayed

schools.summary: Gill: once at ease in affluence and in mind, enjoying God's presence, Job was broken to pieces — substance, family, body, and spirit — the arrows of wrath sticking in him; the Redeemer too, though rich, became poor.

Keil and Delitzsch find the violence in the intensive verbs (to crush, to dash in pieces): God took him by the neck, raised him high, and dashed him down as a mark; Ellicott calls him a St. Sebastian for the arrows of God.
Wesley: God shook him as a strong man shakes a stripling he wrestles with, and set him up for a mark to shoot all his arrows into.

Henry marks the three hard thoughts the dealing bred — that God seemed furious, partial, and cruel — yet corrects them: we must see God directing the arrow, and say, it is the Lord, let him do what seemeth good.

outliers.note: Calls the passage a picture of Job as a St. Sebastian for the arrows of God — hardly possible to conceive a more vivid image of his desolation under the persecuting hand of the Almighty.

themes: I was at ease but he hath broken me
taken by the neck and shaken

schools.summary: Gill lets the archers be Satan's darts, the friends' bitter words, or the diseases of his body, besides the arrows of the Almighty; Job the type of Christ surrounded and shot at on the cross.
Keil and Delitzsch carry the assault to its height, God cleaving Job's reins without pity and pouring his gall on the ground.

Clarke renders 'his great ones' (rabbaiv, though the versions vary between spears and arrows) and, following Heath, finds the huntsman's craft — the beast surrounded, shot, gutted, broken up limb by limb; Wesley: look on our enemies as God's archers, and see him directing the arrow.

Henry: God seemed to touch him in the tenderest part, cleaving his reins (perhaps the pains of the stone) without sparing, pouring out his gall as men gut a slain beast — yet even good men have much ado not to think hard of God.

outliers.note: Renders 'his archers' as 'his great ones' (rabbaiv) and, following Heath, reads the whole picture from the huntsman's craft — surround, shoot, gut, and break up the quarry limb by limb.

themes: his archers compass me round about

schools.summary: Gill: the breaches are the blows that came thick upon his substance, family, and body, one hard upon another, as the first messengers of evil tidings came while one was yet speaking.
Keil and Delitzsch keep the figure of a besieged fortress, God running upon Job like a mighty warrior charging a foe too weak to stand.
Henry: God seemed insatiable, wound after wound with no end in sight, running upon Job like a giant he could not confront — yet this is how affliction appeared to a mind darkened by grief.

themes: runneth upon me like a giant

schools.summary: Gill supposes the sackcloth put on with the rent mantle and the ashes, some reading 'skin' as the thin new skin over a wound; a voluntary humiliation, not mere want of clothing.

Keil and Delitzsch note Job sews the sackcloth on his naked body because elephantiasis would not admit ordinary clothes, and speaks of the scaly surface of the skin; Ellicott reads the first clause figuratively too, the skin grown hard and rugged as haircloth.
Clarke dwells on the horn as the emblem of power (the Abyssinian kirn from Bruce's Travels): to defile or roll it in the dust signifies the disgrace of authority; he rejects Good's 'turban.'

Henry reads deliberate self-abasement: laying aside soft clothing, sewing on the sackcloth to continue his humiliation, laying his horn in the dust — better so than to lift it against Providence and have it broken; against Eliphaz, 'the dust is now the fittest place for me.'

outliers.note: Expounds the defiled horn as the emblem of power from Bruce's Travels — the gilded conical kirn worn on the foreheads of Abyssinian chiefs after victory — explaining the scriptural charges not to lift up the horn.

themes: defiled my horn in the dust

schools.summary: Gill: the word carries the sense of redness (even fermenting red wine), fitting a face grown red and swollen with weeping over his losses, his friends, his corruptions, and the hiding of God's face.

Keil and Delitzsch: the intensive form means the eyes are reddened all over from weeping and so weakened that the shadow of death (cf. ch. 10:21) settles on the lids — yet all this belongs to no disguised hypocrite, as the next verse avows.

Henry: Job banished mirth and set himself to sow in tears, weeping away his beauty and almost his eyes; a type of Christ, the man of sorrows, who blessed them that mourn — his tears wept after a godly sort before the Lord.

themes: my face is foul with weeping
shadow of death on the eyelids
a type of the man of sorrows

schools.summary: Gill: not that Job was sinless, but that nothing in his hands was got unjustly, no property taken, no justice perverted by bribes or accepting persons, as he could challenge any to prove, like Samuel.

Clarke: he asserts with his last breath that the charges are groundless, afflicted unto death but not for iniquity, 'I am no hypocrite, God knoweth'; Wesley: it came not for injurious dealing but for reasons known to God only, and he still prays with a sincere heart (against ch. 15:4).
Ellicott: literally 'for no injustice,' as Isa. 53:9 is rightly read of the innocent Servant; Keil and Delitzsch keep the clause as the ground on which Job dares summon earth and heaven to witness.

Henry makes it the support that held Job up — a conscience void of offence toward men (he despised the gain of oppression) and toward God (his prayer pure, though not sinless, free from reigning guile, unlike prayers made to be seen of men — cf. Isa. 1:15).

themes: not for any injustice in mine hands

schools.summary: Gill reads a self-imprecation: if guilty of blood or oppression, let the earth never cover or conceal it but disclose it, as it discloses the blood of the slain when inquisition is made.

Wesley reads the same — if guilty of destroying any man, let the earth disclose it, and let his cry find no place if this be true; Clarke prefers a call for vengeance, an allusion to Abel's murder, his blood crying against his destroyers as Abel's cried against Cain (Gen. 4:10).

Ellicott: 'let my cry have no place' means let there be no place on earth it does not reach, no resting-place till answered; Keil and Delitzsch set it against the idea that unavenged blood lies bare till vengeance find it (Ezek. 24:7; Isa. 26:21).

Henry holds both senses: if any blood-guilt, let it not be concealed, for the earth shall disclose her blood (Isa. 26:21); but probably Job lays his death on the friends, charging his blood upon them and begging his cry find no place to hide but come up to heaven.

debates.question: What does 'O earth cover not my blood, and let my cry have no place' mean?

sides.position: a self-imprecation — if guilty of blood, let the earth disclose it and my cry find no place
a call for vengeance on his destroyers, his innocent blood crying like Abel's / lying bare till avenged
a cry that must find no resting-place but fill the earth and rise to heaven till answered

themes: O earth cover not my blood
let my cry have no place

schools.summary: Gill: the witness is God himself, the all-seeing dweller in heaven, to whom Job appeals to witness against him if guilty, but for him, as he believes, if innocent.
Clarke: 'I appeal to God for my innocence'; Wesley: besides the witness of conscience, God is witness of his integrity.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'in heaven is my Witness, and One who acknowledgeth me is in the heights'; Ellicott marks the wonder of the confession and its bearing on chapter 19 — faith clinging to the all-just God, knowing One in heaven who ever makes intercession.

Henry: the witness in our bosom avails little without a witness in heaven, for God is greater than our hearts; an unspeakable comfort that God knows the integrity men censure, this one witness instead of a thousand (John 5:37).

outliers.note: Presses the height of Job's faith — what more can the Gospel believer say, who knows One in heaven ever interceding? — his language hovering toward a heavenly witness who is more than the Judge himself.

themes: faith clinging to the all-just God

schools.summary: Gill: they scorn not his afflictions but his words, the arguments he brings in his defence.
Clarke keeps the contrast sharp: 'they deride and insult me, but my eye is toward God; I look to him to vindicate my cause.'
Ellicott would read an apostrophe, 'ye my scorners who ought to be my friends,' the tears running straight into the plea that one might plead for man with God, as he had longed at ch. 9:33.

Henry weighs both cases: helpless before friends who are of counsel against him (their scorn more cutting than enemies'), but his tears found their channel poured out to God, godly sorrow that eases the troubled spirit, which God regards though men slight it.

themes: mine eye poureth out tears unto God

schools.summary: Gill: the wish that one be allowed to plead with God on Job's behalf, or that he plead his own cause, and God decide the controversy — which Job doubts not would be given for him.

Keil and Delitzsch set it among the terms of the trial Job longs for; Ellicott ties it to the daysman of ch. 9:33, the umpire who might lay his hand on both — that one might plead for man with God as the son of man pleads for his neighbour.

Henry sets both readings side by side: a wish for such freedom at God's bar as men have before a magistrate (cf. Isa. 50:8), or the gospel sense the original will bear — one that will plead for man with God, even the Son of man for his friend, on whom we bottom all hope of acceptance.

debates.question: Is 'one to plead for a man with God' merely a wish for a fair hearing, or a foreshadowing of a distinct Mediator?

sides.position: a wish for a fair hearing or an umpire, God himself witness and judge
the gospel sense — a distinct Mediator, the Son of man pleading for his friend

themes: O that one might plead for a man with God
the Son of man our advocate

schools.summary: Gill: man's years are few at best, Job's fewer in his apprehension; 'years of number' are years God has fixed, or that being few are easily counted.

Clarke prefers Good's 'the years numbered to me are come,' Job expecting death every hour, already in its arms; Wesley: 'go' is to depart to the place of the dead whence none return, his death hastening, so he begs the cause be determined.

Ellicott fixes 'years of number' as years easily numbered (as 'men of number,' Gen. 34:20) or allotted; strange for Job to speak of years, which he offers as a hint that the narrative may be an ideal, or that Job speaks simply as a dying man.

Henry: to die is to go the way whence we shall not return, a journey to our long home; we must all shortly go it, and it is comfortable to a good conscience — such that Job could take pleasure in death, sure his everlasting state would be well.

outliers.note: Offers, as no more than a suggestion, that Job's speaking of 'years' in his condition may show the narrative to be an ideal, setting forth the low estate of sin-stricken humanity.

themes: when a few years are come
the way whence I shall not return
death as the crown of integrity
a plea for a speedy hearing
